title: Money Gets Weird
description: Hungary's 1946 hyperinflation, playing-card money in New France and mackerel in US prisons

concepts.title: Hungary 1946: Prices Doubling Every 15 Hours
concepts.contentHtml:
In July 1946 a Hungarian paid in the morning had every reason to spend the money by lunch. That month was the peak of the worst hyperinflation on record: the equivalent daily inflation rate was roughly 207%, with prices doubling every 15 hours.1

Hungary's central bank singles out 10 July as the worst day of all, when prices almost doubled within 11 hours. The cause was the classic one. The war had wrecked the economy, and the government's deficit grew at an accelerating rate while banknotes were issued in ever greater volume.2 Once people expect prices to keep rising, they spend money the moment they get it, and that rush to spend pushes prices up faster still.

The banknotes could not keep up. The record holder, the 100 million b.-pengő note, was worth 100 quintillion pengő, a 1 followed by 20 zeros. Printed in June 1946 and withdrawn on 31 July, it is the highest denomination banknote ever issued.3 To make such sums usable the bank had invented new units: the milpengő, worth a million pengő, and from March 1946 the b.-pengő, worth a million million. A note ten times larger still was planned but never introduced, and when the forint arrived in August 1946, one forint replaced 400 octillion pengő, a 4 followed by 29 zeros.4

A new name alone fixes nothing, so the forint came with a full stabilization program. The government even held back scarce goods so that shop windows could fill all at once after 1 August, and the introduction of the forint became a success.5

concepts.title: Paid in Playing Cards
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1685 the colony of New France had soldiers to pay and no coin to pay them with. The money from France had not come, and the soldiers could not be kept waiting. So on 8 June the intendant, Jacques de Meulles, issued paper money printed on playing cards. He explained to the minister in France that "it occurred to me to issue, instead of money, notes on cards, which I have cut in quarters," and that he had ordered everyone in the colony to accept them.1

The suits meant nothing: a jack of hearts was worth no more than a 3 of spades. Cards were simply the best paper to hand. They were stiff, easy to get, and their plain backs had room for a value and the signatures of officials. Merchants took them on a promise that they would be exchanged for gold and silver coin when a fresh shipment arrived from France.2 Each card was an IOU, worth something only because people trusted that promise and expected others to accept the card in the meantime.

The King disapproved, warning that nothing was easier to counterfeit, and forgers did get to work almost at once. But the colony kept issuing cards, and many were never handed in, because people found them useful as money. That let the government spend more than it had, and by the early 1690s prices were rising. In 1717 the cards were redeemed at a 50 per cent discount and withdrawn.3

They came back in 1729, at the merchants' own request, as plain white cards cut to set shapes: a whole card was worth 24 livres, and one with its corners cut off, 12. Card money circulated on and off until the British conquest in 1763.4

concepts.title: Mackerel, the Prison Dollar
concepts.contentHtml:
When Larry Levine helped a fellow inmate at the Lompoc federal prison in California with his divorce papers, he was paid in fish. A mack is a can or pouch of mackerel, and in much of the federal prison system it had become the standard currency. "A haircut is two macks," Levine told the Wall Street Journal in 2008.1

Prisons always grow some kind of money, because inmates may not hold cash. For decades it was cigarettes. Then a federal rule took effect on 15 July 2004 under which a warden may designate only outdoor smoking areas, and may ban those too.2 Former inmates told the Journal that the mackerel economy dates from about then. A pouch cost about $1, which made prices easy to count, and few prisoners other than weight-lifters wanted to eat it, so the money did not get eaten.3

That is the textbook list of what makes good money: it is durable, standard, easy to get and widely accepted, and few people are tempted to consume it.

Prison money keeps evolving. In 2016 the sociologist Michael Gibson-Light reported on a year in one state prison where packets of ramen noodles, called "soups," had become the currency of choice, even though that prison had no smoking ban.4 He blamed cost-cutting that shrank the meals, so calories became precious. A packet cost 59 cents at the commissary, yet one bought five cigarettes worth $2 and two bought a $10.81 sweatshirt. It is a single prison, so treat it as a case study rather than a census.5

title: Incentives That Backfired
description: The cobra effect and Hanoi's rat tails, a day-care fine that backfired, Mexico City's car ban

concepts.title: The Cobra Effect and the Rats of Hanoi
concepts.contentHtml:
Economists love a story about colonial Delhi. Plagued by cobras, the British rulers offered a bounty for every dead one. People started farming cobras for the reward, so the bounty was scrapped, and the farmers released their now worthless snakes. Delhi ended up with more cobras than before. When the finance professor Vikas Mehrotra told it on Freakonomics Radio in 2012, the man in charge was simply "the British governor, or whoever."1

That vagueness is a clue. The German economist Horst Siebert coined the term cobra effect in a 2001 book of the same name, and there is little evidence that the snake tale is true.2

There is a documented case, and it involves rats. Around 1900 the French gave colonial Hanoi modern sewers, which turned out to be a paradise for rats, and with plague about, the city hired Vietnamese hunters to go down and kill them. On one day in June 1902 they killed 20,112 rats without making a dent. So the city opened the hunt to everyone, paying a cent per rat on delivery of its tail.3

Then people began to notice rats, alive and healthy, running around without their tails. Hunters were cutting off the tails and letting the rats go to breed more, and health inspectors found farms on the edge of the city breeding rats. The bounty was scrapped. In 1906 plague broke out in Hanoi, and at least 263 people died, most of them Vietnamese.4

Both stories run on the same mechanism. A bounty pays for proof of a result, not the result itself, and when proof is cheaper to make than the result, people make proof. Michael Vann, the historian who found the Hanoi records in the French archives, would rename the whole idea: "I'm pushing for the rat effect, in lieu of the cobra effect."5

concepts.title: A Fine Is a Price
concepts.contentHtml:
Every parent knows the closing-time sprint. In 1998 the economists Uri Gneezy and Aldo Rustichini studied 10 private day-care centers in Haifa, Israel, where a teacher had to stay behind whenever a parent was late. For four weeks they simply counted late pickups. Then six of the centers posted a notice: parents who arrived more than 10 minutes late would pay a fine of 10 shekels per child.1

Standard deterrence theory says lateness should fall. It rose. Over the next few weeks late pickups climbed, then settled at almost twice the old rate.2 In the 17th week the fine was dropped without explanation, and lateness stayed just as high.3

The authors' explanation is their title: a fine is a price. Before, a late pickup was a favor from a teacher, with vague and possibly serious consequences, so parents rationed it. The fine told them the worst that could happen was 10 shekels, less than an hour of babysitting, and turned a favor into a service they could buy without guilt. When the fine went, the service stayed bought. In their words, "Once a commodity, always a commodity."4

They do not claim that every fine backfires, and they suggest a large enough fine would probably stop the lateness.5 The lesson is narrower and stranger: a small penalty can do worse than none, because it swaps a moral cost for a cheap price.

concepts.title: The Driving Ban That Bought More Cars
concepts.contentHtml:
Under Mexico City's Hoy No Circula, roughly "today it stays home," a car whose license plate ended in 5 or 6 could not be driven on Mondays. Each weekday banned two final digits, from 5 a.m. to 10 p.m. When the program began in November 1989, it applied to 2.3 million vehicles, or 460,000 a day.1

The logic looked airtight: take a fifth of the cars off the road each weekday and the smog should thin. The economist Lucas Davis tested it with hourly readings from pollution monitoring stations before and after the ban. Across pollutants and specifications he found no evidence that the restrictions improved air quality.2

Drivers had adapted. A household with two cars can drive every day as long as the plates end in different digits. Registrations rose after the ban while new-car sales rose much less, so the program led to more vehicles in circulation and a shift toward used, higher-emitting ones. Nor did people switch to the subway or buses, and pollution rose at weekends and late at night relative to weekdays, as driving shifted to hours when the ban did not apply.3

In July 2008 the city extended the ban to Saturdays. Davis checked again and found virtually no discernible effect on air quality.4 Bogotá has run a similar scheme, and one professor there described his family's answer to it in six words: "We decided to buy two cars."5

title: Bubbles and Manias
description: John Law's Mississippi scheme, Britain's Railway Mania and the great Beanie Baby bubble

concepts.title: John Law and the Mississippi Bubble
concepts.contentHtml:
In January 1720 the man in charge of France's money was a Scottish gambler who had once been sentenced to death. John Law had spent his early adulthood at the gaming tables of Amsterdam, Genoa, Paris and Venice, and in the 1690s, condemned for killing a man in a duel, he had escaped from a London prison. France badly needed a miracle: the wars of Louis XIV had left a state debt of more than two billion livres.1

Law's miracle was paper. In 1716 he opened a bank that issued notes. His trading company, which began by developing France's colony of Louisiana in the Mississippi valley, swallowed its rivals until it collected the taxes, ran the mints and offered the state's creditors its shares in exchange for their bonds. Meanwhile paper notes were to replace gold and silver coins, and Law used freshly created money to hold the share price up. A share that cost about 250 livres in 1718 peaked at 10,000 livres in January 1720, a 40-fold rise, and that month Law became finance minister. The economist François Velde reckons the shares were overvalued at the peak by a factor of 2 to 5. When the scheme unraveled, the money and the shares lost value together.2

Shares changed hands in a narrow Paris street, the rue Quincampoix, which prints of the time show as a crush of speculators, flirts and pickpockets, with Law watching from a window.3 The fall took months, not years. Law, who had promised to cure France's debts, was forced to flee the country in 1720, and he died in Venice in 1729 a poor man.4 The episode still gives economists a lesson about mixing money and markets: a share price held up by printing money stays up only as long as people trust the money.

concepts.title: Railway Mania
concepts.contentHtml:
On 20 September 1845 the comic magazine Punch ran a sketch in which a horrified wife discovers that her husband has become a railway director. Many more lines were being floated than the traffic could support, and many middle-class families sank their savings into new railway companies.1

This was the Railway Mania, and the bust was brutal. The best-known index of railway share prices fell from 167.9 in the summer of 1845 to 60.5 at the end of 1849, a drop of 64%. Charlotte Brontë and her sisters had put most of their small inheritance into one of the lines run by George Hudson, the "Railway King", and lost heavily; Charlotte wrote that "very many" were "by the late strange Railway System deprived almost of their daily bread." Hudson himself was shown in 1849 to have falsified accounts and stolen from his shareholders. Yet the mathematician Andrew Odlyzko, who studies investment manias, argues that fraud was not the main cause. The mania tripled Britain's railway mileage, and the new lines cost more to build and earned less than their promoters had forecast.2

Charles Darwin was in the market too: he bought shares in the London and North Western Railway on 30 June 1846.3 He held on until 1852, when the company's stock crashed during a bitter fight with rival lines. Darwin sold, writing that he took the step "with groans & sighs", and the shares in his wife Emma's trust went at a loss of £587.4 The mania was an investment disaster, but it left Britain a nationwide communication network of great utility, and it was not the last. A second mania in the 1860s added about as much mileage again.5

concepts.title: The Beanie Baby Bubble
concepts.contentHtml:
By the late 1990s some adults were paying up to $2,000 for a small beanbag animal. Ty Inc. kept its most coveted Beanie Babies scarce by "retiring" them, and the craze only grew when McDonald's handed out mini Teenie Beanie Babies in its Happy Meals in 1997.1

Ty Warner created the toys in 1993 and sold them for about $5. What turned a toy into a bubble was a belief that their values would always rise. A self-published author sold more than three million copies of a book of ten-year price predictions, and the magazine Mary Beth's Beanie World reached a million paid copies a month. One advertisement sold plastic lockets for the heart-shaped paper tags under the headline "How Do You Protect An Investment That Increases By 8,400%?", although the tags themselves told owners to remove them before giving the toy to a child. At the peak, Beanie Babies made up 10 percent of all sales on eBay.2

At the end of August 1999 Ty posted a notice that all Beanies would be retired at 11:59 p.m. on December 31, 1999, and many fans suspected a marketing ploy.3 By then the bubble was going flat. "1999 was kind of the end of the dream," says Zac Bissonnette, whose book tells the story: retirement announcements had stopped creating a huge spike in demand. Most Beanies were collected in such vast numbers that few are worth what resale sites claim.4 That is how a bubble works. The price rests on the hope that a later buyer will pay more, and when new buyers stop arriving, scarcity created by a company announcement cannot hold it up.

title: Strange Prices
description: The deadweight loss of Christmas, the hemline and lipstick indexes, and prices ending in 9

concepts.title: The Deadweight Loss of Christmas
concepts.contentHtml:
Your aunt spends $50 on a sweater you would not have paid $30 for. To an economist, $20 of value has just vanished. In 1993 Joel Waldfogel gave this a name in a paper in the American Economic Review: "The Deadweight Loss of Christmas."1 A deadweight loss is value destroyed without anyone gaining it: the shop is paid in full, but the recipient gets something worth less to them than it cost. Waldfogel's surveys found that holiday gift-giving destroys between 10 percent and a third of the value of gifts. Even so, he does not tell people to stop giving. He suggests gift cards, or a donation to charity in the recipient's name.2

The obvious fix is cash, which never misses. So why is it rare? In a 2002 study Waldfogel estimated that Americans give $50 billion to $72 billion of noncash holiday gifts each year, which recipients value at about 10% less than they cost. Givers who tend to pick unwanted gifts are more likely to give cash, which suggests they do care about the recipient, and the rarity of cash gifts fits a stigma attached to handing over money.3 In a 2005 study, people's own purchases produced 10% to 18% more value per dollar than the gifts they received.4

Not everyone accepts the arithmetic. When Waldfogel's 2009 book Scroogenomics called present-giving "an orgy of wealth destruction", critics replied that it ignores sentimental value, and that like other forms of sharing, giving gifts cements social bonds.5 A badly chosen sweater still says that someone thought of you, and the survey numbers leave that message out.

concepts.title: Hemlines and Lipstick
concepts.contentHtml:
When skirts get shorter, the story goes, the economy is booming; when hemlines drop toward the floor, a slump is on the way. This hemline index is usually credited to an economist named George Taylor in 1926. In 2010 Marjolein van Baardwijk and Philip Hans Franses, econometricians at Erasmus University Rotterdam, tested it. They went through the fashion magazine L'Officiel month by month from 1921 to 2009, scored the dresses on five lengths from mini to floor, and compared the result with the official US recession dates. The legend held, with a twist: the economy leads the hemline by about three years, and hemlines show no sign of predicting the economy.1

The lipstick index, coined by Leonard Lauder of Estée Lauder, is the theory that sales of small, affordable luxuries rise in downturns.2 Lauder noticed his company selling more lipstick than usual after the 9/11 attacks hit the economy. But by 2008 the lipstick market itself had fallen on hard times as lip gloss sold strongly, and one chief economist said lipstick would not make his top 20 economic indicators.3 Laboratory experiments suggest there is something to it. In studies by Sarah Hill and colleagues, reminders of a recession lowered women's desire for most products, such as electronics, but raised their desire for products that make them more attractive, which the authors link to attracting a partner with resources.4

Both indexes are folk indicators: memorable stories with a grain of pattern in them. A signal that trails the economy by three years cannot warn anyone of a recession, and lipstick sales follow fashion as well as the business cycle.

concepts.title: The Power of the Left Digit
concepts.contentHtml:
Two used cars are identical except for the odometer. At wholesale auctions, cars showing between 79,900 and 79,999 miles sold on average for about $210 more than cars showing 80,000 to 80,100 miles, yet for only about $10 less than cars showing 79,800 to 79,899.1 A hundred extra miles barely matters, unless it changes the first digit.

This is left-digit bias: we read numbers from the left and pay too little attention to the digits after the first. Nicola Lacetera, Devin Pope and Justin Sydnor found it in more than 22 million used-car sales, with sharp price drops at every 10,000-mile threshold and smaller ones at each 1,000 miles. The evidence points to the final customers rather than the professional dealers at the auctions.2

Shops have long bet on the same quirk with prices ending in 9. Most shoppers do not know what things should cost: in one supermarket study, fewer than half could correctly state the price of an item as they put it in their cart.3 In three field experiments that varied price endings, prices ending in $9 raised demand every time, and the effect was strongest for new items, where customers had the least information.4 Popular origin stories, such as a trick to force cashiers to open the till for every sale, are hard to pin down. One columnist who checked old Chicago newspaper ads found that prices ending in 9 were rare until well into the 1880s and became widespread only in the 1920s.5
